hook: Jordan, 34, feels a pop at the front of his elbow while lifting a heavy box. A bulge appears high on his upper arm. He can still bend his elbow, but it is weak, and turning a screwdriver palm-up is hard. The tendon that attaches the main elbow-bending muscle to his forearm has torn away from the bone, and his other elbow flexors are now doing all the work.

prereq.q: Bending your elbow so your hand moves toward your shoulder is which movement?
prereq.why: Flexion decreases the angle between two bones at a joint. Bending the elbow brings the forearm toward the upper arm, which is flexion. Extension straightens the joint, and abduction moves a part away from the midline.

prereq.q: What attaches a skeletal muscle to a bone?
prereq.why: Tendons are cords of dense regular connective tissue that attach muscle to bone. Ligaments join bone to bone, and a bursa is a fluid-filled sac that cushions where parts rub.

prereq.q: What is a fascicle in a skeletal muscle?
options: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium
The whole muscle wrapped in epimysium
prereq.why: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers surrounded by perimysium. Each fiber inside has its own endomysium, and the epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

anatomy.caption: The shapes of skeletal muscles. Hide the labels and name each fascicle arrangement, then find the belly and the ends that run to the origin and insertion on the spindle-shaped muscle.

chain.cause: Motor neurons signal the fibers of the prime mover.
chain.effect: The fibers shorten and pull on their endomysium, perimysium and epimysium.

chain.cause: The connective tissue wrappings merge into the tendon.
chain.effect: The tendon pulls on the bones at both ends of the muscle.

chain.cause: Fixators and the body's own weight hold the origin's bone still.
chain.effect: Only the insertion's bone moves, pulled toward the origin.

chain.cause: The moving bone turns about the joint, a lever with the joint as its fulcrum.
chain.effect: With the insertion close to the joint (a third-class lever), the far end of the bone moves far and fast, while the muscle pulls several times harder than the load.

chain.cause: To reverse the movement, the antagonist on the other side of the joint contracts.
chain.effect: It pulls the bone back, since the first muscle cannot push.

misconception.wrong: Muscles can push as well as pull, so one muscle can both bend and straighten a joint.
misconception.right: A muscle fiber can only shorten and pull. When it stops, it simply stops pulling. Straightening a bent elbow takes a different muscle on the other side of the joint (the antagonist), or gravity. That is why muscles are arranged in opposing sets across every joint that moves both ways.

summary: Muscles only pull. Each pulls its insertion, on the bone that moves, toward its origin, on the bone that stays still. In a movement, the prime mover (agonist) does most of the work, synergists help, fixators steady the base and the antagonist makes the opposite movement. Bones are levers turning about joints: the fulcrum is in the middle of a first-class lever, the load in a second-class and the effort in a third-class lever. Most body levers are third-class, trading force for speed and range. Fascicles can be parallel, convergent, pennate or circular: pennate muscles are stronger for their size, parallel muscles shorten farther. Muscle names describe location, shape, size, fascicle direction, number of heads, attachments and action.
